core: Definition of oligopoly: a market dominated by a few large, interdependent firms protected by barriers to entry
Why oligopolies exist: barriers to entry and economies of scale that leave room for only a few firms at low average cost
Mutual interdependence: each firm's price, output, and advertising decisions depend on rivals' expected responses (strategic behavior)
Collusion and cartels: firms coordinating to cut output and raise prices; formal cartels vs tacit collusion
Why collusion is unstable (each member has an incentive to cheat) and often illegal (price fixing is per se illegal under the Sherman Act)
A light, correct introduction to game theory and the prisoner's dilemma as the tool for analyzing oligopoly, including dominant strategy
Concentration named as the idea (concentration ratios and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index) without deep treatment
supporting: OPEC as a real international cartel that assigns output quotas and chronically suffers cheating
The ADM lysine price-fixing conspiracy as a real, prosecuted illegal cartel
One-line contrast with the other three market structures (monopoly, monopolistic competition, perfect competition)
outOfScope: Deep treatment of monopoly (economics:foundations:monopoly owns it)
Deep treatment of monopolistic competition (economics:foundations:monopolistic-competition owns it)
Deep treatment of perfect competition (economics:foundations:perfect-competition owns it)
Formal solution of Nash equilibria, mixed strategies, and repeated-game folk theorems
Firm cost curves and the mechanics of profit maximization (economics:foundations:costs owns it)
Full antitrust doctrine and merger-review procedure beyond naming that price fixing is illegal

claims.claim: An oligopoly is a market in which a small number of large firms account for all or most sales in an industry; examples include automobiles, commercial air travel, and cable television.
Oligopolies arise from barriers to entry similar to those that create monopolies and from economies of scale, where market demand supports only a few firms operating at low average cost.
Oligopoly is characterized by mutual interdependence: a firm's decisions about output, price, and advertising depend on the other firms' decisions, so each firm must anticipate rivals' reactions.

Collusion occurs when firms act together to reduce output and keep prices high; a cartel is a group of firms with a formal agreement to collude. In the United States such agreements are illegal, so collusion is often tacit.

Price fixing is an agreement among competitors to raise, lower, maintain, or stabilize prices; it is treated as almost always illegal under the U.S. antitrust laws, with penalties up to ten years in prison for individuals and fines up to $100 million for companies. Agreements to restrict output are just as illegal as direct price fixing.

The prisoner's dilemma explains why collusion is unstable: each firm has a dominant strategy to expand output (cheat) regardless of what the rival does, so rational self-interest drives both to the high-output outcome that yields lower profits than cooperation would.

OPEC, founded in September 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela, is a cartel of oil-producing nations that assigns output quotas to raise prices above competitive levels; individual members have usually exceeded their quotas, illustrating the chronic instability of cartels.

In the mid-1990s Archer Daniels Midland and international partners (Ajinomoto, Kyowa Hakko, Sewon, and Cheil Jedang) ran a lysine price-fixing cartel that raised prices sharply; ADM pleaded guilty and paid a then-record $100 million in fines ($70 million for lysine plus $30 million for citric acid), and ADM executives including Michael Andreas were convicted and imprisoned after an FBI investigation.

Economists measure market concentration with tools such as the four-firm concentration ratio and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI); under the 2023 U.S. Merger Guidelines, a market with a post-merger HHI above 1,800 is treated as highly concentrated.

The four basic market structures are distinguished mainly by the number of firms and product differentiation: perfect competition (many firms, identical products), monopolistic competition (many firms, differentiated products), oligopoly (a few interdependent firms), and monopoly (one firm).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How effective and stable OPEC actually is as a cartel.
positions: OPEC successfully coordinates output quotas to raise oil prices above competitive levels (Zycher, Econlib).
Chronic overproduction and quota-cheating by members repeatedly undermine OPEC's price targets, and some analysts argue it behaves more like a loose political club than a tightly enforced cartel.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses OPEC as a real cartel that assigns quotas AND as the textbook illustration of cartel instability: members' persistent incentive to exceed quotas is exactly the prisoner's-dilemma cheating problem, so both positions reinforce the same teaching point.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact HHI thresholds for a 'highly concentrated' market.
positions: The 2023 Merger Guidelines set the highly-concentrated threshold at a post-merger HHI above 1,800 with an increase of more than 100.
The prior 2010 Horizontal Merger Guidelines used 2,500 and an increase of 200.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites the current 2023 figure (1,800) as a dated, sourced example and treats concentration measurement as a named idea, not a central claim, so the historical change in thresholds does not affect the lesson's substance.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 10.2: Oligopoly
sourceRecords.notes: Core source, read 2026-08-19. Supports: oligopoly as a few large firms with most sales (autos, air travel, cable); origins in barriers to entry and economies of scale; mutual interdependence of output/price/advertising decisions; collusion as acting together to cut output and keep prices high; cartel as a formal collusive agreement; that collusion is illegal in the US and hence often tacit; OPEC named as an international cartel; the prisoner's dilemma and dominant strategy as the analytic tool; the ADM lysine cartel case; and the tradeoff between collusion and competition. Facts only; no wording reused (CC BY-NC-SA discourages reuse).

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 10.1: Monopolistic Competition
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Supports the market-structure spectrum used only for the one-line contrasts: monopolistic competition = many firms selling differentiated products; perfect competition = firms facing a flat (perfectly elastic) demand curve, no market power; monopoly = one firm facing the whole market demand curve. Used to place oligopoly among the four structures, not to deep-teach monopolistic competition. Facts only; no wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: Price Fixing — Guide to Antitrust Laws
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19 via curl with a browser user-agent (the WebFetch fetcher received HTTP 403). Supports: price fixing defined as an agreement among competitors to raise, lower, maintain, or stabilize prices; that a naked agreement among competitors to fix prices is almost always illegal; that penalties include up to ten years' imprisonment for individuals and fines up to $100 million for companies (or twice the gain/loss); and that an agreement to restrict output is just as illegal as direct price fixing. US federal work, public domain; facts used, wording original.

sourceRecords.title: Lysine price-fixing conspiracy
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Supports the ADM lysine case: mid-1990s conspiracy among ADM, Ajinomoto, Kyowa Hakko, Sewon, and Cheil Jedang; prices raised roughly 70% within the first nine months; ADM paid $100 million in fines in 1997 ($70M lysine + $30M citric acid), the largest US antitrust fine at the time; three ADM executives including Vice Chairman Michael Andreas convicted in September 1998 with prison sentences (about 99 months in total, an antitrust record then); Mark Whitacre served as the FBI informant. Cross-checked against contemporaneous press (Washington Post, AP) and a Purdue agricultural-economics case study found in search. CC BY-SA; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Merger Guidelines (2023)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Justice & Federal Trade Commission
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical primary is the FTC/DOJ PDF (issued December 18, 2023); the FTC host and congress.gov both returned 403 to the fetcher, so the specific HHI thresholds were verified through convergent independent summaries (Congressional Research Service product LSB11138, and analyses by Paul Weiss, Skadden, and Stinson) that all state the same figures: a market is highly concentrated at a post-merger HHI above 1,800, with a structural presumption when the merger raises HHI by more than 100 (up from the 2010 guidelines' 2,500 and 200). Used only to name concentration measurement; not central to the lesson. US federal work, public domain.
